chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
title: Rhythms of "Babarabatiri", "Vaya Nina" and "Asia Minor"
summary: He calls these records Afro-Cuban jazz and disliked the double-mambo tempo change on "Asia Minor".

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Macho, what was the rhythm that you recorded "Babarabatiri" for on the Mercury label? Was that a mambo, a guaracha, guaguanco, a son montuno?
It was some, a little Afro-Cuban jazz. It was a fast number, with solos, not as complicated as ahhh, because Rene was very gentle to write. He never used ugly sounds or ...
That was a combination of--- Started with a fast number, raburu buru biri biri, whatever, and then get into the slow thing for a solo, to show a fast pace and a slow pace.
Okay, so what were the combination of rhythms used then?
The same that we used for the Afro-Cuban things, conga, bongo, timbales ......
No, but I mean the rhythm. It wasn't a mambo, it wasn't a guaracha. Was it Afro-Cuban jazz?
Okay, so you were doing mostly Afro-Cuban jazz things then, right?
No, no, no, is a novelty song.
Yeah, but it doesn't fall in the category of son montuno?
No, no, no, no, is a - "Asia Minor" is a number by itself. Is something that this fellow, the composer, create because he is from that particular part of the country, of the world.
But I remember they were doing the double mambo to it then, because the double mambo was popular at that time. Do you remember the double mambo?

Yes, it was a crime to get "Asia Minor" beautiful melody and then the bass, the syncopation of the bass -- Rene put it. It was a crime to change the tempo of things like that. It was so beautiful, because it's a melodic, a flowing melody.
